[[File:Laminar set.svg|thumb|180px|All hyperedges here are either [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] or related by containment. Edge 1 contains edge 4, and edges 3 and 5 contain each other. The set of hyperedges therefore forms a '''laminar set family'''.]]

In [[combinatorics]], a '''laminar set family''' is a [[Family of sets|set family]] in which each pair of sets are either [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] or related by containment.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cheriyan|first1=Joseph|last2=Jordán|first2=Tibor|last3=Ravi|first3=R.|title=Algorithms - ESA' 99 |chapter=On 2-Coverings and 2-Packings of Laminar Families |date=1999|editor-last=Nešetřil|editor-first=Jaroslav |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-48481-7_44|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=1643|language=en|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer|pages=510–520|doi=10.1007/3-540-48481-7_44|isbn=978-3-540-48481-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=2010-07-06|title=Covering a laminar family by leaf to leaf links|journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics|language=en|volume=158|issue=13|pages=1424–1432|doi=10.1016/j.dam.2010.04.002|issn=0166-218X|last1=Maduel|first1=Yael|last2=Nutov|first2=Zeev|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Formally, a set family <math>\mathcal{F} = \{S_1, S_2, \ldots\}</math> is called '''laminar''' if for every <math>i, j</math>, the intersection <math>S_i \cap S_j</math> is either empty, or equals <math>S_i</math>, or equals <math>S_j</math>.

== Construction and Properties==

Let <math>E</math> be a ground-set of elements. A laminar set-family on <math>E</math> can be constructed by recursively [[Partition of a set|partitioning]] <math>E</math> into parts and sub-parts. The [[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] family <math>{E}</math> is laminar. If we partition <math>E</math> into some <math>k</math> pairwise-disjoint parts <math>E_1, \ldots, E_k</math>, then <math>{E, E_1, \ldots, E_k}</math> is laminar too. If we now partition, say <math>E_1</math> into <math>E_{11}, E_{12}, \ldots, E_{1j}</math>, then adding these sub-parts yields another laminar family, and so on. Hence, a laminar set-family can be seen as a hierarchical partitioning of the ground-set into categories and sub-categories.

A fundamental property of laminar set families is that they can be represented as a rooted tree where each node corresponds to a set in the family, and a set <math>S_i</math> is an ancestor of <math>S_j</math> if and only if <math>S_i \supset S_j</math>. This tree representation makes laminar families particularly useful in algorithm design, as many problems can be solved efficiently using dynamic programming on the tree structure.

== Applications ==

=== Hypergraphs ===

The notion of laminarity can be applied to [[hypergraph]]s to define "laminar hypergraphs" as those whose set of hyperedges forms a laminar set family.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rautenbach |first1=Dieter |last2=Szigeti |first2=Zoltán |date=2012-08-01 |title=Greedy colorings of words |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |volume=160 |issue=12 |pages=1872–1874 |doi=10.1016/j.dam.2012.03.038 |issn=0166-218X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Planar Graph Decomposition ===

Laminar families of separators play a crucial role in decomposing [[planar graph]]s. A '''k-separator''' (or k-cutset) in a k-connected graph is a subset of k vertices whose deletion disconnects the remaining graph. For planar graphs, the separators of small size often naturally form laminar families, which enables efficient algorithmic solutions.

Eppstein and Reed<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Eppstein |first1=David |last2=Reed |first2=Bruce |title=Proceedings of the 2019 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) |chapter=Finding Maximal Sets of Laminar 3-Separators in Planar Graphs in Linear Time |date=2019 |pages=589-605 |doi=10.1137/1.9781611975482.37 |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1.9781611975482.37}}</ref> showed that for a 3-connected planar graph <math>G</math>, a [[maximal set]] of laminar 3-separators can be found in linear time. This is non-trivial because some planar graphs like wheel graphs can have <math>\Theta(n^2)</math> 3-separators and <math>\Theta(n^4)</math> non-laminar pairs of 3-separators, making it inefficient to enumerate all separators and then select a laminar subset.

Their algorithm works by transforming the problem: 3-separators in the original graph <math>G</math> correspond to certain 6-cycles in the barycentric subdivision <math>\text{BCS}(G)</math>. The algorithm identifies "frames" (wheel-like structures containing many mutually non-laminar cycles) and handles them separately to avoid quadratic blow-up in complexity. This decomposition has important applications in finding disjoint paths in graphs and computing tree decompositions of bounded adhesion.

Beginning with the work of Wagner,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wagner |first=K. |year=1937 |title=Über eine Eigenschaft der ebenen Komplexe |trans-title=On a Property of Planar Complexes |language=de |journal=Mathematische Annalen |volume=114 |pages=570–590 |doi=10.1007/BF01594196 |issn=0025-5831 |url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN235181684_0114}}</ref> decompositions of graphs by laminar sets of small cutsets have been an important tool in graph structure theory. Wagner showed that every <math>K_5</math>-minor-free graph can be decomposed by a laminar system of cutsets of size at most three into pieces that are either planar or the eight-vertex [[Wagner graph]]. Many similar decomposition theorems are now known, and tree decompositions and [[treewidth]] are also defined by laminar cutsets.
